On the ground of this relationship,

The complainant presented the cheque to her bank i.e. State Bank of India, Sultan Puri Branch however, the same were returned unpaid for insufficiency of funds.
Thereafter, legal demand notice was issued to the accused in regular course, however, she failed to pay the total cheque amount within 15 days thereof and hence the present case.

sentences.text: Legal Position:-
11. The foremost check point is whether the facts averred by the complainant fulfil the basic statutory requirement for constituting an offence under section 138 NI Act.

entities.text: Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh
entities.label: CASE_NUMBER

sentences.text: Being cumulative it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under section 138 NI Act.
12. In the present case, the complainant has filed on record the original cheque as Ex. CW1/A.
The genuineness of the cheques is Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.9 of 19 not disputed.
It is apparent that the accused 'Santosh' is the drawer of the cheques.
The accused has also admitted her signatures on the cheques in question.
Therefore ingredient number (i) stands fulfilled in the present case.
13. The said cheque was presented to the bank within the period of its validity from the date on which it was drawn and was returned dishonoured for the reason "Funds Insufficient".

The returning memo dated 16.01.2014 bearing the fact of dishonour of cheque in question has been Somwati vs Santosh on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/90157792/
5 exhibited by the complainant as Ex. CW1/B.
The returning memo is duly signed and stamped by the bank official.

It is also pertinent to observe here, that during the course of proceedings, the accused had moved an application for discharge on the ground that there was no entry of dishonour of the cheque in question in the statement of account of the accused.
It was argued that the cheque in question was never presented to the bank and the return memo was forged and fabricated.

Ld. 
Predecessor of this court was pleased to dismiss this application vide order dated 17.02.2016, in view of section 146 NI Act, which provides that on a production of a bank slip or memo having thereon the official mark denoting the cheque has been dishonoured, the court shall presume the fact of dishonour.
Thereafter, not even a suggestion to this effect was put to the complainant during her cross-examination.

Moreover, the bank statement brought on record by DW-1 i.e the bank witness clearly shows that cheque return charges were imposed on the accused on 21.01.2014 (i.e.
shortly after the date of return of the cheque Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.10 of 19 16.01.2014).
He further explained that when both the parties have an account in the same bank then in that case no money is debited from the account and the reason for dishonour is mentioned separately.
Therefore, there is no reason to doubt the authenticity of Ex CW1/B.
Therefore ingredient number (iii) & (iv) also stand fulfilled in this case.
14. The complainant then sent a legal notice, Ex CW1/C dated 22.01.2014.
The original postal receipts dated 22.01.2014 has been placed on record as Ex CW1/D & Ex CW1/E along with tracking reports.
I shall observe right here that the tracking reports are not supported by a certificate under section 65B Evidence Act and hence they are not being read into evidence.
Be that as it may, the address mentioned on the legal demand notice is the same as the one mentioned on the bail bonds furnished by the accused.

Since the legal demand notice was properly addressed and posted, it is presumed to have been delivered under section 114 Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter,
"Evidence Act").
Moreover, the accused has admitted receiving the legal demand notice during her statement under section 313 CrPC.

Further, in light of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in C C Alavi Haji v Palapetty Muhammad (2007) 6 SCC 555, the accused not having paid the amount of cheque in question within 15 days of service of summons to him, cannot be allowed to take such a plea.

sentences.text: 15. Now, I shall consider whether condition number (ii) i.e. the requirement that the cheque in question have been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability is fulfilled or not.
Towards this end, it is apt to discuss that a negotiable instrument including a cheque carries following presumptions in terms of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the NI Act.

Section 118 of the NI Act provides :
"Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:
Somwati vs Santosh on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/90157792/
6 (a) of consideration :- that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed,
negotiated or transferred was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;"
Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows:
"Presumption in favour of holder:- it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability"
Thus, the combined effect of Section 118(a) and Section 139 of NI Act raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.

sentences.text: Therefore, existence of condition number (ii) is also presumed against the accused.
Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.12 of 19 16.

sentences.text: When the presumption is raised in favour of the complainant, the burden is shifted on the accused to disprove the case of the complainant by rebutting the presumption.
The accused can displace this presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.
Lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt need not be proved beyond a reasonable doubt as is the general rule in criminal cases.
The accused has to make out a fairly plausible defence which is acceptable to the court.
This the accused can do either by leading his own evidence or by raising doubt /demolishing the material or evidence brought on record by the complainant.

Reliance can be placed on Basalingappa v Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418.
17.

Further, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated.
Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant.

To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist.
The accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence to shift the burden again on the complainant.

[Refer: Bharat Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company v Amin Chand Pyarelal 1999 SCCOnline SC 188 and Kumar Exports v Sharma Carpets, Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.13 of 19 2008 SCC OnLine SC 1885].

Presumption of innocence as a human right needs to be delicately balanced with doctrine of reverse burden contained in section 139 of NI Act.
[Reference can be made to Rangappa v Sri Mohan 2010 SCC OnLine SC 583 and Krishna Janardhan Bhat v Dattatreya G Hegde 2008 (4) SCC 54].

sentences.text: Having referred to the above judicial pronouncements, I shall now analyse the record in their light.
Whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against her.
20. In the present case the main defence of the accused is that she had not taken any loan from the complainant.
At the stage of framing of notice under section 251 CrPC, the accused stated that her husband had given her cheque to the complainant merely as a security.
However, during the cross-examination of the complainant this aspect was completely abandoned and not even a suggestion was put to the complainant in this regard.
Moreover, at the time of recording the statement of accused under section 313 CrPC, she stated that she did not know how the cheque in question reached the complainant.

This shows that the accused has taken contradictory stands during the trial and therefore, her Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.14 of 19 defence does not seem to be reliable.
21.

sentences.text: I have also considered the averments of the accused that the cheque was given as a blank signed security cheque and the same has been misused.

It is trite that averment that a blank signed security cheque has been misused is no defence unless the accused can prove on a scale of preponderance of probabilities that he did not have a crystallized legal liability co-extensive to the cheque amount on the date of presentation of the cheque.

Reliance can be placed on Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar (2019)
4 SCC 197 and Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. v Shruti Investment 2015 SCC OnLine Del 10061.

The accused stated at the stage of framing of notice under section 251 CrPC she had merely given the cheque in question as a security.
However, she not even averred let alone proved on a scale of preponderance of probability the reason why her husband had issued a security cheque to the complainant.

This lacuna is easily explained by the loan agreement Ex CW1/J i.e. the loan agreement between the complainant and the husband of the Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.15 of 19 accused showing that the husband of the accused had taken a loan of Rs 4,20,000/- from the complainant for a period of 11 months.

However, she has neither averred nor proved the same on a scale of preponderance of probabilities.
Counsel for the accused has also tried to challenge the financial capacity of the complainant.
It is trite that in a trial under section 138 NI Act, the complainant is not required to prove her financial capacity at the first instance.

However, the accused has the right to demonstrate that the complainant in a particular case did not have the capacity and therefore, the case of the accused is Somwati vs Santosh on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/90157792/
8 acceptable which he can do by producing independent materials, namely, by examining his witnesses and producing documents.

sentences.text: In the present case during the cross-examination, the complainant has stated that she was not having Rs 4,20,000/- in her bank account on 10.09.2012.
However, the case of the complainant is that she had provided the money in cash and not after withdrawing from her bank account.
Thereafter, she has not been probed at all.
No suggestion has been put to her that she lacked the financial capacity to advance the loan amount.
No suggestion has been put to her that she did not sell any property so as to be in possession of sufficient funds to advance the loan amount.

Most significantly, the complainant has placed on record Ex CW1/J i.e.
the original loan agreement between her and the husband of the accused.
In the said agreement the husband of the accused has admitted taking the loan of Rs 4,20,000/- from the complainant.
This document was never challenged throughout the trial.

Once Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.16 of 19 corroborative evidence of loan transaction itself has been proved and has remained unrebutted, the accused cannot take the plea of lack of financial capacity of the complainant on vague grounds.

sentences.text: 24. I have also considered the argument that the complainant was unable to recall the date of advancing the loan during her cross-examination.
However, this is not a case where nothing has come on record as to the date of advancing the loan.
The date of advancing the loan has been categorically averred in the complaint/affidavit and the complainant has also placed on record Ex CW1/J i.e. the loan agreement.
I am also concious that the testimony of the complainant reveals that she is a lay person.
The case of the complainant cannot be doubted merely because the complainant failed to remember the dates clearly during her cross-examination which was conducted five years after advancing the loan.

25. I have also seen Mark CW1/DA i.e. allegedly the letter sent by the complainant to the Director,
Directorate of education levelling charges of fraud against the husband of the accused.
The complainant has denied sending the letter to the concerned department although she has admitted her signatures on the same.
However, in order to prove that the letter was actually sent/received by the Directorate of Education, the accused could have easily summoned the concerned official.
However, for reasons best known to the accused this was not done.

26. Even otherwise, if I hypothetically assume that the letter was indeed sent by the complainant,
even then, it fails to rescue the Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.17 of 19 case of the accused for the following reasons:-
26.1.

sentences.text: Firstly, the letter has been sent of 04.08.2014 i.e. much after filing of the present complaint and therefore, it cannot subtract anything from the offence alleged to be committed by the accused.

26.2. Secondly, it refers to separate allegations of fraud committed by one Sh. Hari Shankar and Inderjeet forming the subject matter of a separate FIR i.e. FIR No.
573/2014 u/s 420/34 IPC (PS not mentioned in the letter).

It is quite pertinent to observe that name of alleged Inderjeet in Mark CW1/DA is appearing as Inderjeet s/o of Unknown working Govt. Boys Sr. Sec. School, U-Block, Mangol Puri as teacher Somwati vs Santosh on 15 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/90157792/
9 code no. 1412009.
No suggestion has been put to the complainant that the Inderjeet referred to in the letter is also the husband of the complainant.
Quite apparently, the parentage details and address of the person Inderjeet referred to in the letter and the one appearing in the memo of parties is quite different.
The accused could have easily taken some steps to relate the identity of the Inderjeet referred to in the letter, however, for reasons best known to her, no such step was taken.

Even if I assume that the Inderjeet referred to in the letter is the husband of the accused, even then nothing has been elicited in the cross-examination of the complainant as to how the same is relevant for the defence of the accused.

Therefore ingredient no. (ii) remains presumed to have been established against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Conclusion 28.

In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the above discussion, the court is of the considered view that Smt. Santosh is guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, she is hereby convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Upon a prima facie consideration of pre-summoning evidence, cognizance of offence under section 138 NI Act was taken and only the accused Santosh was summoned.
The cheque was not issued towards discharge of any liability or debt.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
12. In the present case, the complainant has filed on record the original cheque as Ex. CW1/A.
Since the legal demand notice was properly addressed and posted, it is presumed to have been delivered under section 114 Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter,
"Evidence Act").
Further, in light of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in C C Alavi Haji v Palapetty Muhammad (2007) 6 SCC 555, the accused not having paid the amount of cheque in question within 15 days of service of summons to him, cannot be allowed to take such a plea.
Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.11 of 19 Therefore, the ingredient number (v) and (vi) are also fulfilled in the present case.
Therefore, existence of condition number (ii) is also presumed against the accused.
When the presumption is raised in favour of the complainant, the burden is shifted on the accused to disprove the case of the complainant by rebutting the presumption.
The accused can displace this presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.
Lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt need not be proved beyond a reasonable doubt as is the general rule in criminal cases.
The accused has to make out a fairly plausible defence which is acceptable to the court.
This the accused can do either by leading his own evidence or by raising doubt /demolishing the material or evidence brought on record by the complainant.
Reliance can be placed on Basalingappa v Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418.
17.
Further, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated.
Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant.
To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist.
The accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence to shift the burden again on the complainant.
[Refer: Bharat Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company v Amin Chand Pyarelal 1999 SCCOnline SC 188 and Kumar Exports v Sharma Carpets, Ct Case No.2837/2016 Somwati v Santosh Page no.13 of 19 2008 SCC OnLine SC 1885].
18. Also, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the defendant-accused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof.
Presumption of innocence as a human right needs to be delicately balanced with doctrine of reverse burden contained in section 139 of NI Act.
[Reference can be made to Rangappa v Sri Mohan 2010 SCC OnLine SC 583 and Krishna Janardhan Bhat v Dattatreya G Hegde 2008 (4) SCC 54].
At the stage of framing of notice under section 251 CrPC, the accused stated that her husband had given her cheque to the complainant merely as a security.
Even otherwise this defence of the accused is not tenable in the eyes of law as a cheque given as a guarantor in discharge of someone else's liability is also covered by section 138 NI Act.
Reliance can be placed on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in ICDS Ltd. v Beena Shabeer,
(2002) 6 SCC 426.
Similar view has also been expressed by the Hon'ble Madras High Court recently in M.
Jaishankar and Anr v Sree Gokulam Chits and Finance Corporation 2020 SCC OnLine Mad 5550.
22.
It is trite that averment that a blank signed security cheque has been misused is no defence unless the accused can prove on a scale of preponderance of probabilities that he did not have a crystallized legal liability co-extensive to the cheque amount on the date of presentation of the cheque.
Reliance can be placed on Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar (2019)
4 SCC 197 and Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. v Shruti Investment 2015 SCC OnLine Del 10061.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Conclusion 28.
In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the above discussion, the court is of the considered view that Smt. Santosh is guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, she is hereby convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
